notes.meaning: God told Moses to go back to Pharaoh, even though the king and his officials were stubborn. God allowed their hearts to stay hardened so He could show His miraculous signs among them. These wonders proved the Lord's great power over Egypt.

differ.view: God sovereignly decided to harden Pharaoh's heart to display His absolute power and justice.
God does not put evil into human hearts, but hardens a sinner by withholding His grace.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: God did not force Pharaoh to do wrong, but permitted him to freely harden his own heart in response to God's deeds.

notes.meaning: God performed these mighty works so the Israelites could tell their children and grandchildren about them. Parents were commanded to teach future generations how the Lord dealt with Egypt. Remembering these acts helps God's people know and trust Him forever.

Moses and Aaron gave Pharaoh a direct message from the Lord God of the Hebrews. God asked how long the king would refuse to humble himself before Him. The Lord demanded that Pharaoh release His people so they could worship Him.

God warned that if Pharaoh kept refusing, a plague of locusts would arrive the very next day. Setting an exact time gave the king an opportunity to repent before disaster struck. Locusts were a dreaded danger that could destroy a nation's crops in a matter of hours.

The coming insects would cover the ground so thickly that no one could see the soil beneath them. They would eat whatever crops survived the earlier hailstorm, including every remaining green tree in the fields. When God chooses to punish a proud land, even tiny bugs can ruin its food supply.

The swarm would crawl into the royal palace and into every Egyptian house, far worse than anything past generations had ever witnessed. After delivering this grave warning, Moses turned around and left Pharaoh's presence without waiting for a reply. Leaving so abruptly showed God's displeasure with the king's stubborn pride.

Pharaoh's own officials pleaded with him to stop fighting Moses. They warned him that Moses was a dangerous trap to their nation and reminded the king that Egypt was already ruined. Even the royal court could see what Pharaoh's stubbornness refused to admit.

Moses and Aaron were brought back to the palace after the officials urged Pharaoh to make peace. The king told them they could go worship the Lord, but then asked who exactly was going. He was looking for a way to give partial consent without letting everyone leave.

Moses answered that the entire community must go, from the youngest children to the oldest elders. They also needed to take all their flocks and herds because they were going to hold a religious festival to the Lord. God's people must serve Him with their whole families and all their possessions.

Pharaoh angrily sneered at Moses, telling them that the Lord had better help them if he ever let their little ones go. He accused them of plotting an evil rebellion to escape his control. He wanted to hold their children as hostages so the men would be forced to return.

differ.view: Satan tries to stop believers from bringing their young children to God, because he opposes early faith.

notes.meaning: Pharaoh insisted that only the grown men could go worship, claiming that was all they had ever asked for. When Moses would not accept this compromise, the king's servants drove Moses and Aaron out of the palace. Pharaoh was willing to make a bargain, but he refused full obedience to God.

The Lord instructed Moses to stretch his hand over Egypt to bring the locusts. The swarm was commanded to devour every plant and herb that the hail had spared. God used Moses' outstretched hand as a visible sign of divine authority.

Moses held out his staff, and the Lord sent an east wind blowing across the land all that day and night. By morning, the wind had carried the vast army of locusts into Egypt. God used the natural wind to carry out His miraculous purpose at the exact time He chose.

The locusts swarmed over the whole country and settled throughout every part of Egypt. There had never been such a terrible horde before, and there would never be another like it. The vast size of the swarm showed that God's power reached far beyond Egypt's borders.

The insects covered the land so completely that the ground turned black. They stripped every plant and all the tree fruit that survived the hail, leaving nothing green in the entire country. God showed that He can easily take away the food and comfort that people take for granted.

Pharaoh panicked and quickly summoned Moses and Aaron back to the palace. He confessed that he had sinned against the Lord and against them by breaking his word. In times of sudden terror, sinners often turn to God's servants for help even when they do not truly love God.

Pharaoh begged Moses to forgive his sin one more time and pray for the removal of this deadly plague. He called the locusts death because they brought total starvation to the country. Yet he cared more about escaping the painful punishment than turning away from his sin.

Moses left the king's presence and prayed to the Lord to show mercy to Egypt. Even though Pharaoh's repentance was hollow, Moses asked God to take away the insects. God showed His great patience by answering the prayer of His servant.

The Lord changed the wind into a powerful west wind that swept all the locusts into the Red Sea. Not a single insect remained in any part of Egypt. God proved that all winds and weather obey His commands just as easily to show mercy as to send judgment.

As soon as the relief came, the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and the king refused to let Israel go. God confirmed Pharaoh in the stubborn path the king had repeatedly chosen. Rejecting God's warnings over and over leaves a person trapped in their own rebellion.

The Lord commanded Moses to raise his hand toward the sky so that a thick, heavy darkness would fall upon Egypt. The darkness was described as something that could be felt, like a damp fog. Because Pharaoh broke his word, this punishment struck suddenly without any advance warning.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest God used a severe desert dust storm, known as the khamsin, to create this dense darkness.

notes.meaning: Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and a total blackness covered all of Egypt for three full days. The dense gloom wiped out normal daylight, and indoor lamps could not pierce the heavy air. This was a clear defeat for Egypt's sun god, proving the Lord alone rules the heavens.

The Egyptians were so terrified that they could not see each other and remained frozen in place for three days. Meanwhile, the Israelites enjoyed light in their own homes and villages. God made a clear separation between the house under His curse and the people under His blessing.

Pharaoh called for Moses again and offered to let the children go along with the adults. However, he insisted that their cattle and sheep must stay behind. The king still wanted to keep a hold on the Israelites by holding their property as security.

Moses firmly turned down Pharaoh's condition and told him the king must even provide animals for their sacrifices. Israel needed animals to offer burnt offerings to the Lord their God. God's ministers cannot compromise His commands to satisfy an earthly ruler.

Moses declared that every single animal had to leave with them, without leaving behind a single hoof. They needed their herds for worship, and they would not know which sacrifices God required until they arrived. God requires His people to dedicate all their belongings to His service.

The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart once again, and the king refused to let the people leave. Instead of bending to God's demands, Pharaoh became completely unwilling to give up his prisoners. Pride led the king to keep fighting against God to his own ruin.

Pharaoh flew into a rage, ordering Moses to get out of his sight and never return. He threatened to kill Moses the very day he saw his face again. Blinded by fury, the king threatened the very prophet who had prayed to save his land from earlier plagues.

Moses accepted Pharaoh's words, stating that he would never appear before the king again. Moses knew that the next judgment would finally force Pharaoh to let Israel go without any more negotiations. When a sinner drives away God's truth, God leaves them to face the consequences.
